# Decision Record on Batch Caching and Notifications

This record initially placed Batch null Caching and Notification consumer Lifecycle in the same compatibility window. The shared window still makes sense: both issues left points in the regression materials that need checking, and neither can be closed out based on a single surface symptom. However, the window is a planning arrangement, not an explanation of the mechanism.

The initial draft's working hypothesis was a convenient one: after tracing the cache entry point to clarify null handling, the differences observed in the notification scenario might become easier to explain. That hypothesis was not retained after review. The two tracks can appear in the same round, but no material shows that one causes the other. The current decision is not to look for a single shared cause, but to document the judgments we can make separately for each subject.

`LoadingCache` is the starting point for the batch track, not evidence that it is responsible for the notification lifecycle. The frozen path is `jetcache-core/src/main/java/com/alicp/jetcache/LoadingCache.java`, the file is in the `com.alicp.jetcache` package, and `CacheEvent`, `HashMap`, and `LinkedHashSet` are directly visible at the top. These names are enough to indicate that a review should examine how each key in a batch request is retained, how results are collected, and whether the nearby event-related code is actually used by the call sites; the names themselves cannot determine the semantics of storing null.

Three approaches to documenting this were compared at the time.

| Approach | Issue | Decision |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Treat both issues as a single compatibility defect | Would turn an unconfirmed causal relationship into a conclusion | Rejected |
| Look at `LoadingCache` first, then also infer the consumer state | The cache file can provide a local entry point, but cannot substitute for observations from the notification scenario | Rejected |
| Record them separately while retaining the shared regression window | The release context is retained, and neither judgment stands in for the other | Adopted |

This choice has a direct consequence: regression records cannot contain only "window passed" or "window failed". Record observations for the batch path and the notification path separately. If one still lacks inputs or results, records from the other cannot be used to fill in its record.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> CompatibilityWindow
    CompatibilityWindow --> Batch_null_cache
    CompatibilityWindow --> Notification_consumer_lifecycle
    Batch_null_cache --> LoadingCache_review
    Notification_consumer_lifecycle --> ConfigurationSnapshotCheck
    LoadingCache_review --> SeparateRecords
    ConfigurationSnapshotCheck --> SeparateRecords
```

The two branches in the diagram merely show the recording order used on this page. It does not depict the consumer's internal state machine, nor does it show `CacheEvent` as a confirmed link between the two tracks. Previously, placing the two pieces of work side by side made it easy to read "both appeared in the same regression round" as "they must follow the same implementation path"; that reading is no longer used.

## Batch Track

The review entry point for Batch null Caching remains `LoadingCache.java`. First, we need to distinguish three observations that may all be loosely called "null caching": the result returned by a batch call contains null; the result container retains null; the corresponding value can still be seen in a subsequent read. These are not the same thing. The first observation only tells us about that particular call's result; only after actually observing a subsequent read can we go on to discuss cache state.

`HashMap` and `LinkedHashSet` make this entry point worth examining first, but should not be overinterpreted. The former may hold intermediate results, while the latter may retain each key from the request; the actual call sites still determine their roles in the batch path. The relationship among loader, key, and value must also be confirmed at the actual reference sites; we cannot infer nonexistent behavior from class or import names.

One statement in the early records was later withdrawn:

> When null appears during a batch read, the notification-side anomaly can be interpreted as part of the same round of cache invalidation.

This statement turned simultaneous observations into causality. The existing materials do not provide the complete relationship from batch reads to notification processing, so withdrawing it does not mean another cause has already been found. The decision retained for the batch side is narrower: in each regression round, first clearly identify whether the observation concerns the call result, the result collection, or a subsequent read; none of the three can stand in for the other two.

This also means this page does not prescribe any particular null sentinel, container implementation, or loading strategy. These have not been confirmed in the existing materials. What the compatibility window needs is a record that can be reviewed later, not unobserved implementation details presented as the standard explanation.

## Notification Track

The scenario for Notification consumer Lifecycle needs its own record. Here, at a minimum, "lifecycle" must not be conflated into one general state: whether a consumer appears, whether it receives a notification, and whether it enters the processing stage are different questions. Without the inputs and outputs from the configuration snapshot, we can only retain "inconsistent results in the observed scenario", not arbitrarily pick one stage as the cause.

JCR-223 is the navigation entry point for the notification track. A counterexample was added to that card on 2025-10-21; its specific mechanism is not detailed in the materials on this page, so no channels, connections, or processing order are invented here. The records retained afterward only confirm that one point in the Notifications and Broadcasts section remains unconfirmed, with the inputs and outputs kept in the configuration snapshot. This counterexample is enough to overturn the early shared hypothesis: even if the cache side is explained first, that does not automatically make the notification side certain.

One condition is also retained for the notification scenario: in an environment with no old cache and no personal configuration, check the paths where creation does or does not occur. This condition applies only to the notification track. It is not a prerequisite for Batch null Caching, nor can it be rewritten as an environment requirement for every regression run. Its purpose is to prevent old cache or personal configuration from confounding the assessment of whether a consumer appears.

`CacheEvent` appears at the top of the `LoadingCache` file and can still serve as a pointer for further investigation of nearby event-related code; it is not evidence of completed consumer creation, consumption, or closure. The fact that both the cache code and the notification materials mention events is not enough to assign the consumer lifecycle to this file.

## Decisions Retained After Review

JCR-206 moved into review on 2025-09-22, on the grounds that implementation had been completed on an existing branch; a support scenario was linked the next day. What can be confirmed here is that the change entered review and a support entry point appeared; "completed on an existing branch" cannot be read as meaning that Batch null Caching has been fully validated in every environment.

Accordingly, JCR-206 serves on this page as a navigation reference and review context for the batch track, not proof of sign-off. The support scenario can help revisit the conditions at the time, but does not replace the distinction between batch calls, result collections, and subsequent reads. If only one result from the support scenario is available, the record should stop at that result rather than extending it into a conclusion about all batch paths.

The following decisions were ultimately retained in this round:

- For Batch null Caching, review the code around batch reads in `LoadingCache`, recording call results, result collections, and subsequent reads separately.
- For Notification consumer Lifecycle, check the inputs and outputs in the configuration snapshot, and observe the paths where creation does or does not occur with no old cache and no personal configuration.
- Two observations may be logged in the same regression round, but the pass, fail, or unconfirmed status of one cannot be copied to the other.
- `CacheEvent` is retained only as a pointer to nearby event-related code, not as a conclusion that the notification lifecycle has been implemented or validated.
- JCR-206 and JCR-223 are retained as navigation entry points for the batch review context and the notification scenario, respectively.

This decision does not isolate the two issues into unrelated pieces of work. They still share the compatibility window for R2026.09, and may be discovered together in the same regression run. Cross-references, however, refer only to the shared time window and regression batch, not to any unconfirmed causal relationship.

The missing pieces should also be left where they are: this page contains neither specific call samples for Batch null Caching nor the contents of the configuration snapshot. If subsequent work confirms that there are direct references between the batch path in `LoadingCache` and event handling, add the actual locations and the inputs for that run; if there is no direct relationship, the shared window remains only release context. For the related Annotation context Parsing and Notification process hook, see also DOC-16.

# Annotation Parsing and Notification Interface Proposal

For this discussion, treat context parsing on the annotation side and Notification process hook as one concern: once the caller has obtained the cache object, pass enough context along to the notification path. This keeps the trial scope small and avoids having to guess the cache name and annotation constants independently in two places.

We're leaning toward adding a thin entry point alongside `jetcache-anno/src/main/java/com/alicp/jetcache/anno/support/CacheManager.java` first. That file is under `com.alicp.jetcache.anno.support`, and its only visible dependencies are `Cache` and `CacheConsts`. This is a good place to retrieve and pass along context; the notification side would only consume the prepared data, without going back to interpret the annotations.

The risk is that context may serve more than just notifications. If we later find that cache regions, cache names, or expression processing are also used by other paths, keeping parsing on the manager side would lock in the boundary too early. Another option is to have Notification process hook retrieve the values itself, but that would create two sets of parsing logic for the same annotation across different entry points.

Don't merge the two types of entry points yet. During the trial, look only at the creation path; existing caches and personal settings can mask whether parsing actually happened. The rollback conditions are simple too: if the hook needs to add a second set of annotation interpretation logic, or we can't explain where the context it receives comes from, back out this merge attempt.

# Annotation Parsing and Notification Interface Proposal

This trial draft retains the early view that "context parsing and Notification process hook should be on the same path." The question at the time wasn't the notification format, but who should pass the information already known on the annotation side to downstream processing. The initial draft treated `CacheManager` as a nearby place to start: the file is at `jetcache-anno/src/main/java/com/alicp/jetcache/anno/support/CacheManager.java`, and its visible declarations bring in `com.alicp.jetcache.Cache` and `com.alicp.jetcache.anno.CacheConsts`. This isn't enough to establish where the implementation belongs, but it does show that the discussion at the time didn't start with the broadcast implementation itself.

The initial proposal was to assemble the annotation context as early as possible, then pass it to Notification process hook. That way, the notification side wouldn't need to reinterpret the cache region, cache name, or annotation constants; new entry points could also reuse the same context. The trade-off was that the manager side would take on an additional responsibility that hadn't yet been confirmed. At the time, "context is only for notifications" was a provisional assumption; the other annotation entry points hadn't been examined individually.

## Disagreements Remaining After Review

JCR-207 later described the issue as inconsistent results from Annotation context Parsing at user sites, and called for checking the creation and non-creation paths in an environment without old caches or personal configuration. This check shifted the focus of the trial: previously, the concern was how the object would be passed into the hook; during review, the higher priority was to confirm whether context appeared reliably in a clean environment. A design comparison was recorded on the card, but its results were not written up as an implementation conclusion that could be adopted directly.

JCR-224, by contrast, checked Notification process hook in a clean working directory, focusing on exit codes, file changes, and leftover directories. This check and JCR-207 are not interchangeable. The former shows the result of the annotation entry point; the latter shows whether any working directories that shouldn't remain are left after processing ends. The two were originally combined into a single trial to reduce the scope of changes; looking at it now, that arrangement would conflate parsing failures with an unclean state left after processing.

The two candidate boundaries therefore remain, but they no longer have to land together:

- **Parse early.** `CacheManager` or an adjacent entry point generates the context once, and Notification process hook only receives the result. This is suitable for checking whether the content is consistent for the same annotation entry point, but which fields actually belong in a general-purpose context needs to be clarified first.
- **Let the processing side fetch what it needs.** The hook uses the cache object and annotation information it receives to perform the necessary interpretation. The change looks localized, but can easily lead to parsing rules being duplicated at another entry point; this is only suitable for checking whether the hook already has enough information.
- **Don't connect them yet.** First run the two clean-environment checks separately, record the creation path and leftover directories, then decide whether a shared object is needed. This choice doesn't resolve the interface shape; it only avoids using one result to vouch for the other.

The earlier statement that "the notification side shouldn't go back and interpret annotations" remains here as the preference at the time, not an established constraint. In particular, the available material has no conclusion on whether empty expressions, cache-name derivation, and instance identity are already determined on the manager side. If these only hold for a particular annotation entry point, generating a general-purpose context early would instead widen the scope of errors.

## Trial Sequence

First reproduce the paths covered by JCR-207 in an environment without old caches or personal configuration. Record whether creation occurs; don't include existing-cache hits in the assessment. Then run the processing associated with JCR-224 in a clean working directory, recording observations of the exit code, file changes, and leftover directories separately. If both rounds can be completed, compare them to see whether they need the same context; don't add a shared interface without this comparison.

Two types of failure are acceptable during the trial. The first is that the creation path doesn't yield enough of a result to make an assessment. In that case, stop discussing the hook's parameters and return to the annotation entry point. The second is an abnormal process hook exit or directory state. In that case, don't attribute the problem to the parsing logic, and don't continue merging just because the context looks complete. Roll back the corresponding trial for each type of failure; don't use a change on one side to cover the other.

Withdraw the "parse early" option if a second set of fields needs to be added specifically for notifications, or if the same field has to be generated by different rules at different annotation entry points. Withdraw the "let the processing side fetch what it needs" option if the hook reinterprets annotations to obtain information and that interpretation has already diverged from the one at the preceding entry point. After withdrawal, retain `CacheManager` as a reference location, but don't treat it as the sole home of the notification logic.

## Still Open

- What is the minimum content of context, and does it include annotation information beyond the cache object?
- Can the process hook handle only one invocation, or does it need to recognize repeated entries for the same cache object?
- When file changes and leftover directories occur, are they related to notification processing, or are they left by the execution entry point itself?
- If both checks pass, should the interface have the annotation side provide an object, or only an identifier that can be queried again?

This record may still be overturned by later field results from JCR-207 or JCR-224; when citing it, consider it alongside the check conditions on both cards, rather than taking only the early judgment to combine them.

# Jedis cluster and channel decision record

This page initially grouped the Jedis cluster factory and channel opt-in in R2026.09 Compatibility Window together because they repeatedly came up together in the same round of compatibility discussions. The earliest decision, however, was not to combine the two into a single implementation task, but to leave separate completion criteria for each: for the factory, whether the inputs could form an adequate configuration closure; for the channel, whether callers actually had a visible entry point.

The early investigation began with `jetcache-starter/jetcache-autoconfigure/src/main/java/com/alicp/jetcache/autoconfigure/JedisPoolFactory.java`. This file's package name is `com.alicp.jetcache.autoconfigure`, and the only types that appear directly at the top are:

```java
import org.springframework.beans.factory.FactoryBean;
import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Autowired;
import redis.clients.jedis.Jedis;
```

The old notes therefore placed it on the starter auto-configuration side, rather than initially classifying it as an ordinary cache or broadcast manager. This positioning is still useful: it provides a starting point for reading near the factory. The early notes' statement that "the review can be completed from the pool factory alone" is retained as the working assessment at the time. The filename, package name, and three direct dependencies are not enough to show which configuration items the cluster inputs pass through, nor can they replace the actual reference relationships.

## Closeout approaches compared at the time

There were two approaches at the time. One was to treat channel as a capability that naturally followed from factory configuration: investigate the Jedis factory first, then mark channel as available as well. The other was to acknowledge that the two shared a compatibility window, but assess them separately. The latter was ultimately adopted.

The reason was not that channel and configuration had no connection at all, but that the two issues were missing different information. The question for the cluster factory concerned inputs and configuration closure; the question for channel opt-in was whether callers could opt into the broadcast channel. Using the factory's progress to draw a conclusion about channel would hide the caller entry point behind internal configuration checks; conversely, using entry-point discussions to fill in the factory's configuration closure would also record unconfirmed input relationships as already resolved.

The old draft stated this decision very briefly: continue looking at starter on the factory side, and retain a separate entry point on the channel side. Later readers could easily misinterpret this as describing two entirely unrelated features. The boundary actually retained was narrower: they could appear in the same compatibility review and share the same Jedis time window; they simply could not share a single completion signal.

## Follow-up notes on the factory track

JCR-211 narrowed the original, fairly general investigation goal to: check the configuration closure involved in the Jedis cluster factory changes, and return to the corresponding repository file for each missing item. This changed the earlier reading approach. `JedisPoolFactory.java` is still an entry point, but is no longer treated as the closure itself.

Later records categorized this issue under failure_classified and explicitly recorded, "One part of the Jedis cluster factory is still unconfirmed." This information invalidated the earlier optimistic closeout. It did not specify whether that part was a field, a constructor branch, or a runtime result; this page does not fill that gap with seemingly precise implementation details either. What is certain is that the factory file's direct dependencies alone cannot close out this item.

The caller issue was later handed over to the person responsible for interface compatibility for confirmation. The handoff itself indicates that further assessment needed clarification from a compatibility perspective; it does not mean that ownership of the starter implementation had changed, nor that the unconfirmed part had disappeared. If the handoff in the old page was read as meaning "the factory has been confirmed," this follow-up note takes precedence: the unconfirmed part remains, and what changed is the entry point for further checking.

At the time, there was also consideration of recording all missing items as Jedis client issues so they could be grouped with other compatibility matters. This consolidation was not adopted. Gaps in the configuration closure need to be traced back to the repository locations where something is actually missing; generalizing them as client issues would instead cause later reviews to bypass the original factory path.

## Separate record for the channel track

JCR-228 focuses on the user-visible entry point for channel opt-in. The checking approach it leaves is to trigger the corresponding job through the existing automation entry point, and retain the job, commit, and actual artifact name. This requirement is not about adding an internal parameter description to the factory, but about enabling callers to recognize whether opt-in appears.

There was subsequently one design comparison. The surviving material does not retain the full details of the candidate implementations, nor does it preserve the name or artifact contents of a particular job, so this page does not supply a passing result after the fact. Only one decision can be retained from that comparison: channel opt-in continues to be handled as a separate entry point and cannot be absorbed into input confirmation for the Jedis cluster factory.

There was once an easier sequence: look at the factory first, then assume channel would appear along with the configuration. This sequence was later abandoned. The problem was not that there was no technical connection whatsoever, but that the sequence had taken the place of the actual things being checked: the factory track needed to confirm configuration closure, while the channel track needed to confirm the caller entry point and the results left by automation. Establishing the former does not automatically establish the latter.

Interface discussions about the broadcast prefix and Redisson broadcast manager are recorded separately in DOC-21. DOC-21 can explain why a separate comparison was made on the broadcast side, but should not, in turn, add direct responsibilities to `JedisPoolFactory.java`, nor can they fill the factory gap left in JCR-211.

## Decisions still in place

This history does not provide the final form of the cluster factory inputs, nor does it define channel's default behavior. # Broadcast Prefix and Manager Proposal

R2026.09 For this round, do not treat the broadcast prefix as an incidental parameter of the regular cache configuration. The trial is to make the prefix used by broadcasts independent and provide an explicit registration point for the Redisson broadcast manager. These two items are discussed in the same round because both affect invalidation notifications for multi-level caches; they do not need to share a configuration object, and they should not be coupled automatically just because they use the same remote client.

There are currently two candidate directions.

- Continue using the existing cache-side prefix and have the broadcast manager reuse it directly after obtaining the configuration. This has a small change surface, but callers cannot distinguish cache-key naming from broadcast-channel naming; once a cache region needs a different channel prefix, the configuration semantics become mixed together again.
- Define the broadcast prefix separately and read it when the manager is registered. This adds another configuration entry, but keeps channel naming within the broadcast boundary. The Redisson adapter only needs to care about that entry and manager construction; it does not need to derive the channel from a regular cache name.

The preference is to try the second approach first. Here, "independent" refers only to the configuration and naming boundaries; it does not mean adding another cache-key rule set, and it should not incidentally change the regular cache construction path. The Redisson broadcast manager is not a replacement for the existing manager registry; it is one broadcast implementation that can be selected from the registry. The registry retains its manager-facing role, and Redisson Adapter stays at its own integration point to avoid scattering client checks through cache-region configuration.

The verification entry point is currently `jetcache-starter/jetcache-autoconfigure/src/main/java/com/alicp/jetcache/autoconfigure/RedisAutoConfiguration.java`. The file header shows direct dependencies on `CacheBuilder`, `CacheConfigException`, and `ExternalCacheBuilder`, making it a suitable starting point for reviewing configuration assembly and exception handling. The file being in the starter module only indicates that it is worth checking; whether it is responsible for actually constructing the Redisson manager still needs to be confirmed by tracing references before deciding.

For the trial, check only three outcomes: after specifying only the broadcast prefix, the cache-side prefix remains unchanged; when it is not specified, no second naming scheme is generated out of thin air; and the Redisson broadcast registration can coexist with the existing manager registry. If any one of these requires the regular cache configuration to know about Redisson, or requires putting the channel prefix back into the cache name, drop the separate entry, retain the existing prefix path, and handle the manager registration separately.

What remains undecided is where the default value should live, and whether missing configuration should cause startup to be rejected or fall back to the existing broadcast naming. The former affects how explicit callers must be, while the latter affects upgrade cost within the compatibility window. First add the Redisson broadcast repository tests and capture the current failure output, then decide the default behavior; until then, do not write the trial conclusion as a general configuration constraint.

# Jackson Conversion and Broadcast Troubleshooting Tree

This page originally came from a file found in a search. The search terms included Jackson key conversion, another incident record mentioned Spring Data Broadcast Adapter, and the earlier investigation simply grouped the two under the same entry point. A later review first changed this order: the file path is still retained, but attribution must wait for runtime results and object relationships to become available, and cannot be inferred from the issue name.

```text
Anomaly observed
├─ A. Jackson key conversion
│  ├─ Actual return value obtained
│  │  └─ Record the input, unmodified return value, type, and usage location
│  ├─ Exception obtained
│  │  └─ Record the exception type, full message, and first identifiable location
│  └─ Only a search hit or file path available
│     └─ Stop at the entry point, do not infer the runtime chain
└─ B. Spring Data Broadcast Adapter
   ├─ Failure during configuration setup
   │  └─ Save the triggering configuration and original error
   ├─ Failure when sending a broadcast
   │  └─ Save the result of the publish action
   └─ Failure during reception or decoding
      └─ Save the received content and exception boundary
```

## First Confirm the Evidence You Have

The first line of an on-call record is often just "anomaly after upgrade" or a search result. Both can point to the same file, but they do not support the same conclusions. Actual runtime results must answer at least three questions: what object was passed in, what was returned or thrown, and where the anomaly occurred. If all you have is a path, just record the path and the object to investigate; do not present hit counts or filenames as evidence of a fault.

Branch A especially needs to distinguish key from value. A result that looks like a conversion failure does not mean that the input was necessarily a key. First paste the input unchanged next to the result, preserving quotation marks, null values, and type information. When the return value differs from expectations, first write "different result", rather than immediately stating that Jackson key conversion has failed. If `CacheEncodeException` appears during the incident, do not compress the full exception into "encoding failed"; the exception type and message are the starting point for later determining the encoding boundary. When there is no exception and only a return value, do not replace the observation with an exception name either.

The direct dependencies currently visible in the file header are as follows:

```java
import com.alibaba.fastjson.JSON;
import com.alibaba.fastjson.serializer.SerializerFeature;
import com.alicp.jetcache.support.AbstractValueEncoder;
import com.alicp.jetcache.support.CacheEncodeException;
```

These declarations confirm that there is a local entry point for the Fastjson value encoder here, and can also help trace back the object being encoded and the exception type. They cannot by themselves identify the caller of key conversion, much less confirm that broadcast messages pass through this class. If reproduction yields only a value encoding result, retain the result, then look for the location where a key is actually passed in; if all you have is the file header, stop at the file entry point and do not invent a call relationship.

## Branch A: Where the Conversion Result Ends Up

After obtaining the returned content, first check whether the input and output belong to the same run. Do not reformat the returned content for readability, and do not remove null values. If the conversion result has already been used downstream, also record the usage location separately from the result: the former shows who took the value, while the latter shows what this entry point actually produced. If neither is available, Branch A must remain pending investigation.

When you obtain an exception, retain the full message and the first section with an identifiable location. If the exception is located in the value encoder, this only shows that this run failed at the encoding entry point; it does not imply a failure in broadcast sending or on the receiving side. If the exception is located elsewhere, do not relocate it here just because `FastjsonValueEncoder.java` turned up in the incident search. Older records placed "file found in search" before "whether runtime results are available", and that assessment can still serve as a historical lead, but the troubleshooting order is now reversed.

If the same input yields different results in different environments, first save the original content from both sides side by side. A result changing from a value to an exception calls for a different approach from a result changing from a value to empty content; do not lump them together as "inconsistent environments". The current material does not identify a specific caller, so the call relationship remains limited to what the runtime output can actually point to.

## Branch B: Determining the Stage of Broadcast Integration

Anomalies after upgrading Spring Data Broadcast Adapter must first be classified by stage. Failure during configuration setup means that, at a minimum, the incident cannot reach the point of observing a send; successful configuration setup with no business effect does not directly imply that nothing was published; receiving content but failing to decode it must not be described as the sender not working either.

If failure occurs during configuration, save the configuration that actually triggered it and the error, and do not change the encoder yet. If failure occurs during sending, save the original result corresponding to the publish action, and separately record whether anything was observed on the receiving side. If a message was obtained during reception but had no business effect, keep the message content, reception result, and business behavior separate; if an error is thrown during decoding, retain the received content and exception type, and do not substitute "had no effect" for a decoding exception.

When all you know is "post-upgrade regression", retain that scope and do not arbitrarily label it as configuration, sending, reception, or decoding. If a downloadable artifact is also obtained during a review, record the artifact separately from the failure stage as well. The existence of an artifact does not mean it already contains a fix; without an explicit object name, do not fill in a version number or an assumed recovery package.

## File Entry Point and Environment Comparison

The currently frozen entry point for follow-up investigation is:

`samples/simple-samples/src/main/java/FastjsonValueEncoder.java`

The path is recorded in `internal/cache-interop`'s `v_prev`. When tracing back, first inspect the file header and its immediate neighbors at the same revision, then place the runtime results back in their corresponding environment. Do not retroactively write an entry point found in a later search into the old path, or expand a path annotation into a claim of implementation ownership.

For environment differences, record only what can be verified on both sides:

- Whether the same input produces the same returned content;
- Whether the return value becomes an exception, empty content, or no result;
- Whether the broadcast failure occurs during configuration, sending, reception, or decoding;
- Whether the artifacts obtained before and after the upgrade are the same.

If only the environment was changed and the original results from both sides were not saved, this comparison cannot determine the stage. "Works locally, fails in production" can only be recorded as an observation, not as a substitute for the input, output, and failure location. If results appear on only one side, first mark the side that is missing, rather than assuming that the other side performed the same action.

## Boundaries of Recovery Actions

Earlier troubleshooting records noted that switching back to the old entry point still produced no output. This shows that this recovery action yielded no observable result, but it is not enough to declare the old entry point incompatible; you still need to confirm whether the input, output, and broadcast stage were actually captured at the time. Without an execution result, record only "attempted to switch back", not "recovery failed".

After recovery, the original observations must be repeated. For Branch A, repeat the same input and save the result unchanged; for Branch B, repeat the original configuration or publish action, and inspect sending, reception, and decoding separately. If recovery only changed the entry point without changing the environment or input, those conditions must still be recorded next to the results, otherwise the before-and-after results cannot be compared directly.

```text
Result available ──> Compare input and stage ──> Continue investigating object relationships
   │
   └─ No result ──> Retain the entry point and gaps ──> Do not attribute a cause
```

## On-Call Stopping Points

1. Only an issue name, call name, or file path, with no runtime output: stop at the entry point.
2. `FastjsonValueEncoder.java` was observed, but the input has not been confirmed as key or value: stop at object identification.
3. The broadcast has no business effect, but whether a send occurred has not been confirmed: stop at the sending boundary.
4. Only a post-upgrade failure, with no failure stage: retain "post-upgrade regression", and do not specify a recovery target.
5. The exception message is truncated: obtain the original exception again, rather than substituting a summary.

What this page can currently confirm is the file entry point, the local dependencies, and that the two symptoms should be handled separately. The assessment of who actually calls Jackson key conversion, whether Spring Data Broadcast Adapter connects to this value encoder, and exactly which stage the broadcast stops at can only be updated once the corresponding runtime records are available.

The links between the file path, issue name, and call name can serve as a starting point for searching; where the implementation resides must still be verified separately against the file contents and the actual usage context.

## The Initial Placement

In the spring of 2025, this object's naming and the file path were closely linked. The search terms from the earlier investigation included `starter`, `config`, `configtree`, `getproperty`, `string`, `environment`, and `value`, so looking first at `ConfigTree.java` in the auto-configuration directory was a reasonable search step. The problem arose in the next step: a search step could easily be written up as a conclusion about where the implementation belonged.

There were not many options for handling this at the time:

| Option | What could be preserved at the time | Underlying issue |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Base the conclusion on the filename | Immediately identify an implementation location | Conflates the entry point with the consumption point |
| Write nothing for now | Wait until the full relationships and a reproduction are available | The earlier investigation cannot continue to be used |
| Record the entry point and gaps | Preserve material from portions of the file and questions pending verification | The page will not prematurely make a final determination of where the implementation belongs |

Use the third option. This is not because the information was already complete, but because the materials available at the time were only sufficient to support a limited decision. The page can explicitly record where the file is, which types appear in its header, and how earlier records point here; it cannot go on to claim which object obtains the string value, nor can it claim that this value has already been returned by a user call.

This choice also affects "History" in the title. What is recorded here is how the assessment narrowed from "it looks like it is right in ConfigTree" to "start by checking ConfigTree", rather than presenting an unresolved object relationship as a formal definition. The strong assertion on the old page is retained to explain why the position had to change later; it is no longer presented alongside the current position as though both were valid conclusions.

## Facts limited to the file header

The declarations preserved in the header of `ConfigTree.java` are:

```java
package com.alicp.jetcache.autoconfigure;

import org.springframework.core.env.ConfigurableEnvironment;
import org.springframework.core.env.EnumerablePropertySource;
import org.springframework.core.env.PropertySource;
```

The package declaration places the file in the `com.alicp.jetcache.autoconfigure` namespace. It can help readers confirm the file's relationship to the group of names associated with starter auto-configuration, but the package name itself does not answer which object ultimately uses the string property.

`ConfigurableEnvironment`, `EnumerablePropertySource`, and `PropertySource` are direct dependencies visible in the file header. They provide three type clues to check first when reading through the file: an environment object, an enumerable property source, and a general property source. The available materials do not preserve any snippets showing calls involving these types within a method, nor do they preserve the result returned after a value is obtained, so the page keeps them alongside the file entry rather than arranging the three into an execution chain.

"Direct dependencies" here is a description at the file-header level. It is not a substitute term for runtime relationships. For example, seeing `ConfigurableEnvironment` lets you continue looking for where environment properties are read; seeing `PropertySource` lets you continue checking how property sources are accessed; but these two names alone cannot justify assigning the file a caller that has not been shown. These limits are not a separate set of explanations, but the reason this page limits its record to the file header.

| Materials on hand | Assessment that can currently be retained | Unresolved object questions |
| --- | --- | --- |
| File path | Start tracing back from `ConfigTree.java` | Whether it is the final point of consumption |
| `package` declaration | The file belongs to `com.alicp.jetcache.autoconfigure` | Whether the package name corresponds to a runtime owner |
| Three import statements | The file header contains type clues for the environment and property sources | Which method actually obtains the string |
| Pointers from the earlier investigation | The issue name and call name can lead readers back to this path | Whether the earlier pointers already cover the complete call relationships |

This table only breaks out four kinds of evidence; it does not turn gaps into new conclusions. It also explains why the earlier page can continue to be cited: the entry-point information remains valid; what no longer holds is the step of directly equating the entry point with ownership.

## A Review That Was Not Completed

In the activity history for JCR-216 on 2025-10-06, the reproduction was first moved from To Do to Blocked. The specific reason recorded was that the read-only account needed for reproduction was still pending approval. Around 15:20 that day, the work was moved back from Blocked to To Do, because online issues would be handled first this cycle and it would be scheduled for the next cycle.

This history contains no reproduction result. It cannot be polished into "verified failure," nor can it be written as saying that a configuration value was empty, erroneous, or successful. The only thing that can be confirmed is that the reproduction conditions were not ready within that handling window, after which the work was returned to the to-do list.

The card also contains another correction in a public comment from the same day: in the Starter Configuration section, there is also one unconfirmed point concerning ConfigTree String Properties. Here, the "correction" addresses the page's tendency to state the file location too definitively. It does not provide the object name, caller name, or return value for that point, so the page continues to leave it unconfirmed rather than filling in a name for it.

The earlier TODO can therefore be broken down into four distinct gaps:

- whether a local declaration exists inside the file that directly corresponds to the string-property retrieval action;
- whether `ConfigurableEnvironment`, `EnumerablePropertySource`, and `PropertySource` all actually participate in that action;
- which routine user call passes through this relationship;
- whether that call can leave a return value or raw diagnostics.

These four items do not share a single answer path. The first and second require returning to the local code in the file; the third requires finding the usage path; the fourth requires a review artifact that can be retained. Collapsing them into "To be confirmed" would make it unclear to the reader which layer to check next, so they are kept separate for now.

## Change in the Review Method

The local description of JCR-216 requires that "ConfigTree String Properties" be exercised through a routine user call rather than a debug entry point, with the return value or raw diagnostic retained. This requirement concretely changes the verification procedure, but it does not automatically make `ConfigTree.java` the final consumption point.

The current review is treated as two consecutive steps: first, start from the file entry point to check local declarations and property source relationships, then place the same object back in the context of the user's routine calls and observe what results can be retained. The first step answers "what relationships are present in the file", and the second answers "what path is taken during use". A debugging entry point can at most provide intermediate observations, not replace the routine calls in the second step.

"Retain return values or raw diagnostics" also has a clearly defined scope here: the actual return values observed must be retained, or unprocessed diagnostic material must be retained. The current page has no such samples, so "should be retained" is not written as "has been retained". There is also no material indicating that approval for the read-only account was later completed, so the blocker encountered that autumn cannot be retrospectively rewritten as a successful reproduction.

If review results become available in the future, they should align with the local relationships in the file. Having only a new issue name, the same old link, or another occurrence of this path still only shows that the lookup entry point has not changed; it does not automatically resolve the object relationships. This distinction is the practical purpose of retaining the autumn record in the current version: it explains why the page still has empty entries, rather than manufacturing a failure case.

## Options Compared and the Decision

**Option One: Treat file location as implementation ownership.**

This is closest to the initial intuition. Readers can get a short answer just by seeing `ConfigTree.java`, and maintenance costs are low. But it treats the navigation results from the earlier investigation as call relationships, and import names as read operations that have already occurred. If it were later found that another object retrieves the string properties, the entire page would have to be retracted, so this option was not adopted.

**Option Two: Wait until all relationships are confirmed before saving the page.**

This approach avoids premature conclusions, but would lose the paths, package names, and file-header dependencies that are already valuable. Those revisiting the earlier investigation still need a location that leads back to the source file; waiting for everything would also fail to explain the misreading at the time. A complete pause was not adopted.

**Option Three: Record only the card, not the source file.**

The card can specify the requirements for routine calls and retaining results, but it cannot replace the file path. Saving only the card would tell readers how to conduct the review, but not where to start reading. This option was not adopted either.

**Option Four: Retain the entry point, and separate ownership from results.**

This is the current decision. The file path, package declaration, and three direct dependencies are retained as entry-point material; the objects retrieving string properties, the consumers, and the return values are retained as items awaiting verification; routine calls and raw diagnostics are retained as review conditions. This option does not provide the shortest single-sentence conclusion, but it matches the level of detail in the available material.

Choosing Option Four also entails a practical compatibility cost: readers need to examine both the file level and the call level, rather than judging by filename alone. This cost is acceptable, because the more convenient alternative wording would cement unconfirmed relationships in the knowledge base. When new results are added in the future, object relationships or diagnostics only need to be added at the corresponding gaps; there is no need to delete the existing entry point and earlier judgments.

## Decision Outcome

The current position is fixed as follows:

- `jetcache-starter/jetcache-autoconfigure/src/main/java/com/alicp/jetcache/autoconfigure/ConfigTree.java` remains the verification entry point for ConfigTree String Properties.
- `package com.alicp.jetcache.autoconfigure;` in the file header is retained as file location information.
- `ConfigurableEnvironment`,`EnumerablePropertySource`,`PropertySource` are retained as direct dependencies and pointers for inspection.
- The navigation links from issue names and call names to this path in the earlier investigation remain valid.
- Paths, package declarations and import statements do not by themselves establish ownership of the complete implementation.
- When neither a return value nor a raw diagnostic sample is available, do not record a run result.
- Rechecks should prioritize following routine user calls, rather than only observing the debug entry point.

The decision here concerns how the documentation records existing decisions and the order of the next verification steps, not a decision to modify the code implementation. The existing material provides no basis for the claim that "changing `ConfigTree.java` alone is enough to complete the compatibility window", nor does it identify another owner that can be named directly. This page therefore records the file entry point separately from the ownership assessment.

## Path diagram

The state diagram below includes only verification nodes already mentioned on this page, and does not indicate an execution order among the three import statements:

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> FileEntry
    FileEntry --> LocalDeclarations
    LocalDeclarations --> RoutineUserCalls
    RoutineUserCalls --> ReturnValueOrRawDiagnostics
    LocalDeclarations --> UnconfirmedRelationship
    ReturnValueOrRawDiagnostics --> [*]
```

"UnconfirmedRelationship" in the diagram corresponds to the object relationship that is currently still missing, not to an already named code object. "ReturnValueOrRawDiagnostics" in the diagram corresponds to the recheck artifacts that JCR-216 require retaining; it is not marked as already existing. The purpose of the state diagram is to separate the entry point, in-file checks, routine use and result retention, and it must not be treated as evidence of a call chain.

## Order of use for recheck entry points

When given an old issue name or call name, first return to `ConfigTree.java` under `internal/cache-interop`, and confirm the package declaration and the direct dependencies in the file header. Do not jump directly from the filename to implementation ownership. Then look within the local scope of the same file for the operation that retrieves the string property; if the local material still cannot establish the object relationship, retain "UnconfirmedRelationship", and do not substitute a module name for an object name.

After obtaining a result for the local relationship, check whether routine user calls pass through it. Routine calls here are not another name for the debug entry point, and it must be possible to explain how a call reaches that object. If a value is observed, retain the return value; if there is no value but raw diagnostics are produced, retain the original diagnostics. If neither is available, the page can only record that the recheck produced no output, and must not label the absence as success or failure.

No specific name for the routine call entry point is currently provided, nor are there any return values, raw diagnostics, or caller code snippets. This gap must remain in the document, because filling in a seemingly reasonable name would change the factual scope of the event record. Read-only account approval and the prioritization of production work explain why the previous round stopped, but they are not a guarantee of subsequent results.

## Why the old judgment is not deleted

The earlier statement that "processing should be in the ConfigTree section" is no longer the current conclusion, but it still has historical value. It shows where the misreading originated: the search terms simultaneously matched starter, configtree, environment, and value, and the file header did in fact contain a Spring property-source type, so the file location looked like an answer about where it belonged.

If this statement were deleted outright, later readers could see only the narrowed position and would not know why it is necessary to distinguish the entry point from the consumption point. Retaining the original text and correcting it afterward shows what counterexample triggered the change in understanding: the file path and type declaration did not provide the caller, return value, or raw diagnostic. This is not using hindsight to correct the early author, but putting the old judgment back in its original context, when the available information was insufficient.

Similarly, the fall blocking record is not rewritten as "review failed." The reason for the block was read-only account approval, and the reason for returning to the backlog was to handle production issues first; neither describes the runtime result of ConfigTree String Properties. The current decision uses them only to explain why the review was not completed, and does not derive a technical conclusion from the state transition.

## Items not yet closed

1. The local location of the action that retrieves the corresponding string property in `ConfigTree.java`.
2. The actual relationship at that location between `ConfigurableEnvironment` and the two property-source types.
3. The specific entry point used by the user's routine call and the caller object.
4. A verifiable return value or raw diagnostic.
5. Whether the review can answer the first four items once the read-only account conditions are met.

These items cannot substitute for one another. Finding the file location completes only the first layer of navigation; confirming an import does not automatically produce a return value; and obtaining one observation from a debugging entry point still cannot satisfy the routine-call requirement. When content is added next time, the new material should be placed under its corresponding item, while preserving the path and the early judgment on this page.

## Adjacent material

JCR-216 is the only card on this page that requires direct navigation. It narrows the review from "looking at a particular debugging location" to the user's routine call and requires preserving the return value or raw diagnostic. The card does not provide a caller name or result, so it addresses only this local requirement.

DOC-26 is an adjacent interface review within the same compatibility window. Its subject is Lettuce topology refresh, not ConfigTree String Properties. The two pages can serve as navigation for each other within the same window, but the interface assessment from DOC-26 must not be moved into this page, nor should this page's file header be used to explain the connection relationship on the other page.

## Current stopping point

The final decision retained on this page is: continue using `ConfigTree.java` as the verification entry point, withdraw the strong claim that the file location alone establishes complete ownership; use the package declaration in the file header and descriptions of the three direct dependencies to describe the local context; use routine user calls, return values, or original diagnostics to define the observable artifacts for the next review; when there is no evidence for object relationships and results, explicitly leave blank entries.

This is already sufficient to support continued follow-up of the earlier investigation, and it does not disguise a single path as a complete implementation description. If an actual call relationship is found later, that relationship and the corresponding result should be added; if the same path or issue name is obtained again, the current decision on this page remains unchanged.

# Lettuce Topology Refresh Proposal

The earliest records only categorized the issue in R2026.09 Compatibility Window under Lettuce topology refresh; only later was the actual investigation narrowed to a single file. The investigation still starts with `jetcache-support/jetcache-redis-lettuce/src/main/java/com/alicp/jetcache/redis/lettuce/RedisLettuceCache.java`, but this is only the existing starting point. It does not establish that the file is responsible for creating or triggering refresh, or for its results.

The following can be checked in the file header:

```java
package com.alicp.jetcache.redis.lettuce;
import com.alicp.jetcache.*;
import com.alicp.jetcache.external.AbstractExternalCache;
import com.alicp.jetcache.support.JetCacheExecutor;
```

These declarations show that it sits alongside the Lettuce cache implementation. `AbstractExternalCache` and `JetCacheExecutor` are direct dependencies. This does not justify inventing method names that are not there, or treating connection initialization, connection reuse, and topology refresh as the same operation. The earlier draft treated the file's location more as evidence of responsibility. That assessment should remain in the history, but this revision no longer uses it as a premise for the proposal.

## Candidates Under Consideration

The first candidate is to trigger refresh near the existing Lettuce connection reuse entry point. It is closer to the point where "the old call fails," and the trial scope is narrower. The downside is that an old call may reuse a connection before triggering a topology update; if the terminal only records a final status, we cannot tell whether the failure occurred during connection reuse or refresh. The trigger point for this candidate cannot be considered found just because the paths are adjacent.

The second candidate is to trigger it near connection initialization or where configuration is applied. This places the operation at a more clearly defined initialization boundary, making it easier to compare behavior before and after initialization. The cost is that all instances going through that entry point could be affected, and ordinary cache users may not need this refresh; if the issue only occurs with old calls, broadening the initialization scope would also turn the compatibility window into a connection behavior change. The available material does not establish that this entry point exists, so it remains only a candidate.

There is also a variant that leaves the trigger location unchanged: first continue tracing back through the file's declarations and adjacent Lettuce objects to confirm which object the old call actually passes through, then choose where to run the trial. This variant will not directly resolve the failure, but it avoids mistaking a file path for a call relationship. If tracing back still does not locate the actual trigger point, the search should not casually expand to the manager registry, annotation context, or other cache backends.

## Verification Steps

The later entry-point description from JCR-217 was: run "Lettuce topology refresh" through the entry point users normally use, and save the terminal output and workspace side effects separately. This provides a verification action, not a conclusion that an implementation location has been established. The available material also does not include the full output of this run, so it cannot be reduced here to a single confirmed success or failure for refresh.

The two types of records need to be examined separately. The terminal may show that the call failed while the workspace has no changes within the same scope; alternatively, the call may not report an error immediately even though the connection state has already changed. The former does not directly establish that the workspace operation failed, and the latter does not establish that the topology has refreshed merely because no exception occurred. At a minimum, trial records must retain the entry point, the verbatim terminal output, and the observed workspace side effects individually. They cannot be replaced with a single "refresh succeeded."

This revision does not adopt the approach of "change just one configuration value and see what happens." Changing configuration alone may make it look as though refresh took effect when in fact the connection was simply re-established; replacing the entire Lettuce initialization path outright would introduce even more connection behavior. A smaller trial should hold the user entry point and existing cluster setup fixed, and observe only whether a refresh action occurs, the terminal output, and workspace side effects. "Fixed" here is a condition for comparison, not a commitment already made about the current implementation.

## Points Still Open After Review

The earlier draft favored triggering refresh near the connection because it was close to where the issue occurred. After review, that rationale supports only the first candidate, not a final decision. If the actual trigger point is in an adjacent object, the proposal should shift to that location; if the action can only be observed at the initialization boundary, the impact scope must also be reassessed. We cannot keep strongly attributing this to `RedisLettuceCache` just because the issue name and call name once pointed there.

How to handle failure output is also undecided. Trial code should not turn an exception into a success result or report compatibility conclusions without corresponding workspace records. The existing records do not settle the exception type, the exact changes in cluster URI, or compatibility differences between Lettuce entry points; we cannot turn them into interface constraints in this revision.

## Rollback Boundaries

If the added refresh handling causes connection initialization to fail, or introduces behavior in ordinary cache paths that was not there before, first remove the added entry point and restore the original connection path. If terminal output cannot be matched to workspace side effects, also stop expanding the trial first, and do not use retry results to determine the cause. After rollback, retain the failure output and the file locations already rechecked. These materials can support the next investigation, but cannot be used to infer that the cause of the original failure has already been established.

This revision can therefore support a localized comparison of candidates, but cannot serve as the authoritative description of the current Lettuce topology refresh implementation. The next actual verification needs to first fill in the object relationships along the old call path, then choose between the two locations; until then, the initialization location, reuse location, and specific exception remain undecided.

# Troubleshooting Tree for Stalled Runtime Observability

When runtime observability stops progressing from the "current entry point," branch based on the objects visible in the live state. Follow only one branch at a time; if there is no evidence for the preceding step, stop there rather than treating a guess as the root cause.

## Entry branches

- If you can still find `annotation context` on the page or in the output, first note its corresponding `source id`, then follow that object back to review `jetcache-core-operations-observability`. Do not clean up the live state or retry first.
- If you only have `cache area` and no `annotation context`, preserve the raw content and check whether it can still be matched to the current entry point. If it cannot, stop and hand off to the permissions owner; do not infer object relationships from names.
- If the entry point displays `Lettuce connection`, first record it as a connection-related clue alongside the live state, not as grounds for concluding that there is a connection failure. A new trace or version information is needed to continue.

## When evidence is available

1. You can see `source id`, but there is no subsequent topology information: stop at this node and preserve the first failing sample, run id, trace, and version.
2. You have seen `topology refresh`: confirm whether it occurred after this entry-point action. If there is no event ordering or trace, stop here as well; do not substitute a historical successful sample for this observation.
3. You have `ordered key`, but `monitor lifecycle` has not advanced to the next step: record the `cache area` containing the key and the location of the first anomaly, then hand off through the Runtime Observability project's maintenance entry point. Do not keep guessing about the caller here.
4. You only have a permissions error, restricted details, or unreadable attachments: record the visible error and entry-point address, then hand off directly to the permissions owner. Do not perform recovery actions until the permissions issue is resolved.

## Stopping and handing off

Stop if any of the following occurs: the first failing sample has been overwritten; the current entry point can no longer be matched to `source id`; the ordering of `topology refresh` is unclear; there are only screenshots and no trace to review; or runtime observability is now showing a permissions error. Include the raw sample, run id, trace, version, and the branch reached in the handoff. Do not state an unverified final cause.

Earlier records show that retrying too soon made it difficult to compare the original failing sample and environment differences. Preserve the first failure before deciding whether to retry. Recovery actions have not yet been validated in the shared environment; if the behavior after a retry differs, save both results separately without overwriting the original record.

This page only covers branches after entering runtime observability from the current entry point. Do not fold input replay in adjacent projects, caller integration testing, or other cache issues into the same tree.

# Compatibility Directory Entry Migration Index

Migration records begin at `docs/adj-jetcache-anno/migration/current-entry-legacy-entry-migration-index.md`. Similar-named side paths are not folded in here; each item corresponds only to the legacy entry left in the compatibility directory, its replacement location, and the callers still using that entry.

The directory covers public contracts formed around schema and API. A legacy entry is not deleted immediately just because a new location appears in the directory: calls to Fang Ke can still read records from the old location, or only part of the compatibility adjustment may have been completed. Migration is considered complete based on confirmation from actual users, not on whether the new entry has appeared in the directory.

## Filling in the Index

Each legacy entry keeps its own record, which must state at least:

| Record item | Content to retain |
| --- | --- |
| Legacy entry | Original name and current status; entries that can no longer be traced back remain marked as expired |
| Replacement location | The location to switch to now, and whether it carries compatibility content for schema or API |
| Callers | Callers still using the legacy entry; if no caller has been confirmed, do not mark the item complete |
| Migration status | Not started, in progress, confirmed, or legacy entry restored |
| Exit criteria | The item's own completion conditions and maintenance plan |

Old records may remain in the directory. Their purpose is to tell callers where they originally entered, not to treat expired content as the current contract. Do not supplement information that cannot be traced back with guesses, and do not mark it as migrated merely because a replacement location exists.

## Migration Order

Start with one legacy entry, verify the schema or API contract associated with it, and then identify the callers still using it. Once it is confirmed that the callers can switch to the replacement location, update the status of that record; if callers in the same batch use different entries, record them separately rather than replacing item-by-item confirmation with a directory-level rollup.

The replacement location only carries compatibility content that has already been confirmed. If callers need to retain the legacy entry, keep the record "in progress" and note that the legacy entry is still in use. The new location in the directory and the callers' actual switch are two different things; the former cannot be used to conclude the latter.

Each item has its own schedule, maintainer, and exit criteria. The index records migration relationships only; it does not promise a shared completion time for neighboring items in a single record. Callers that have not yet been confirmed remain under the original entry; change the status once a usage result is available.

## Returning to the Legacy Entry

When the replacement location can no longer meet a caller's needs, first restore that caller to the corresponding legacy entry, then change the index status to "legacy entry restored." Do not delete the replacement location or erase the migration record that already exists; keeping the record shows which compatibility relationship the restoration occurred on. After restoration, the public contracts for schema and API must still be rechecked, so that a single caller rollback is not incorrectly recorded as the entire directory abandoning the migration.

Restoring the legacy entry affects only callers confirmed to need restoration. Other entries with confirmed migrations remain at their respective statuses until their own exit criteria are met.

The judgments about `async timeout`, `null sentinel`, and `Jedis client` in the old tree came from early samples; they can still help identify old incident states, but cannot establish the cause of a new incident. In particular, the "hand off if there is no `Jedis client`" exit path has since proved problematic because missing records and permission denials can also lead to the same exit.

## First Pin Down the Object Under Investigation

Before following a branch, write down the current entry point, the version identifier for samples-client-integration, the original input, and the first visible result. Here, the first means the first record after the current revision changed, not the earliest one of the day or the easiest one to inspect after rerunning. JCRD-003 preserves this checkpoint; a later green result only shows that a later attempt succeeded, and cannot replace the first sample.

If it has not yet been confirmed whether the current revision was actually captured or executed, keep the status unknown. Do not mark it as "executed" because the page has an object with the same name, someone remembers running it, or later results are normal. JCRD-005 was left for this gap: it provides no conclusion, and only prevents an unknown status from being treated as confirmed during handoff.

Objects with the same name must also be separated first. The gap addressed by JCRD-004 is that references to samples-client-integration did not clearly identify the version; when an older object and the current object with the same name are mixed together, any inputs, permission information, or results obtained afterward cannot be meaningfully compared. At this point, do not enter the root-cause tree, and instead supply the identifiers first. If the identifiers cannot be supplied, stop at object confirmation.

```text
Current entry point is stuck
│
├─ Cannot find the original record
│  └─ Record the input, current revision, and first visible result
│     └─ Stop: do not discuss root causes or assign someone to take over
│
├─ Original record exists, but the object version is not clearly identified
│  └─ Separate the older object from the current object with the same name
│     ├─ Version can be confirmed: return to the original-record branch
│     └─ Version cannot be confirmed: stop at object confirmation
│
└─ Both the original record and object version are available
   ├─ Access through the standard entry point is denied
   │  └─ Preserve the point of denial and request/run id
   │     └─ Check the permissions entry point first, then decide whether a permissions owner is needed
   ├─ Unclear whether execution occurred
   │  └─ Keep the current revision's status unknown, and supply evidence of capture or execution
   └─ Execution is confirmed and the stuck state can be reproduced
      ├─ Someone other than the author can reproduce it using the original steps
      │  └─ Continue comparing integration samples and environment differences
      └─ Only the original author can reproduce it
```
